chunks.heading: The Cycle of Us
chunks.notes: Introduces the nine-lives frame and depicts the first life's drowning sacrifice, ending on a peaceful, almost transcendent death image.

chunks.heading: The Cycle of Us
chunks.notes: Grandson narrator recounts the father's addiction and estrangement, his reconciliation and death, and the birth of daughters who continue the family line, centered on the memorial bench.

chunks.heading: The third Life
chunks.notes: Third life narrator recounts a car crash that kills the father and one sister, the surviving sister's suicide attempt witnessed as a child, and later reconciliation with the mother.

chunks.heading: The third Life
chunks.notes: The soul-line's fourth life is a restless man running from an inherited ache and an unease around the ocean he can't explain, framed explicitly as the soul "shedding" rather than dying.

chunks.heading: The third Life
chunks.notes: The fifth life settles into a mechanical desk-and-clock routine described as a punishment, with a fragment-stacked list before an unexplained longing cracks the monotony.

chunks.heading: The third Life
chunks.notes: The sixth life's unrequited love confronts inherited abandonment wounds and ends with the brother's soul-line dissolving into the next form.

chunks.heading: The third Life
chunks.notes: The seventh life (sister's first stage) chases dream-visions that feel like memories of a person she never met in this life, realizing dreams are doorways rather than destinations.

chunks.heading: The third Life
chunks.notes: Covers the end of the eighth life's solitary garden years through the ninth life's healed, forgiving old age on the sea-bench, closing with the explicit line "It's alright now."

chunks.heading: The third Life
chunks.notes: The closing two lines explicitly reveal the "presence" as the entire chain of past-life selves rather than a ghost, tying back to the opening frame of nine shared-faced people.
